title: How do you handle consistent scaling between AI-generated game assets?
author: Private_Tank
selftext:
I'm currently working on a game where I generate buildings and other assets using AI. I've run into a problem with scaling that I hadn't really considered before.

My current approach is to generate an image at roughly the right dimensions for the plot size. Then I take the visible building, crop it, and center it on the plot. For example, for a 2x2 plot, I use a 512x512 image, with each plot being 256x256 pixels.

This actually works surprisingly well. The buildings fit their plots nicely, and the results look pretty good.

**However, I've noticed a major problem:** every asset gets scaled independently, so there's no consistent scale between different buildings.

For example, I have an apartment building and a much larger skyscraper. If I scale both to fit their respective plots, their proportions relative to each other can look completely wrong. A door on a regular apartment building might end up looking huge compared to a door on a skyscraper.

I'm trying to figure out the best way to solve this without losing the benefits of my current approach.

Some ideas I've considered:

* Defining a standard reference size, such as a door or a floor height, and scaling all buildings relative to it.
* Assigning target dimensions to each building category.
* Including reference objects and explicit size constraints in the AI image generation prompts.

But I'm not sure which approach works best in practice, especially when generating lots of assets automatically.

**How do you handle this in your own projects?**

Do you define a global scale for all assets and let some buildings occupy only part of their plots, or do you use another approach? And how much of this can realistically be solved through prompting versus post-processing?

I'd appreciate any advice or examples from people who have dealt with a similar problem.

PS: In the image, all rectangles are the same size to show the problem off even moire

comments.author: Significant-Neck-520
comments.body:
What are you using to generate the art? Local models ot gemini/ chatgpt. I suppose it wont matter much for this technique tough.
What I tried to make for tileable textures was to add the 8 surrounding tiles I wanted and then keeping the center of the canvas masked to be the only editable place. I think that you could have an area 3 times the size of the sprite you want to create, and add art in the perspective you want to be used, then requesting the empty space to be filled. The model will try to copy the perspective and art style, hopefully, maybe.

comments.author: United-Tour5043
comments.body: u use a proper 3d model as the basis for generating the asset.

comments.author: Rsouss
comments.body: The problem isn't the assets. From what I see, you're giving both the same lot size. Smaller houses need smaller lots, and larger buildings need more lots. That way it's proportional.

comments.author: DeProgrammer99
comments.body: I chose not to worry about it. Frankenstein scaling isn't even unusual in game design. Look at the size of StarCraft marines vs. Battlecruisers, which hold thousands of personnel.

comments.body: Also build the systems first with placeholder graphics and then near the end, generate the final graphics so the API has an easier time keeping things consistent.
